title: Water
intro: Your tap water in Edenvale travels from dams in Lesotho, through the Vaal system, to Rand Water's treatment plants, then through Ekurhuleni's pipes to your flat. It is tested against a national standard and Ekurhuleni scores well. The weak spot is supply, not quality, so the smart moves are a small water store and, if you want better taste, a simple filter.

sections.title: Where your tap water comes from
points: Edenvale falls under the City of Ekurhuleni. City outage notices list Edenvale among the areas it supplies.

The journey starts in Lesotho. The Lesotho Highlands Water Project (a joint Lesotho and South Africa scheme) stores water in the Katse and Mohale dams and sends it through tunnels into the Vaal River system.
The Vaal system is a network of 14 linked dams. Rand Water takes its raw water from the Vaal Dam. Sterkfontein Dam is the backup and only tops up the Vaal Dam if it drops below 18%.

Rand Water is the bulk supplier. It cleans the water at big plants like Zuikerbosch in Vereeniging: it adds lime so dirt clumps and sinks, filters it through sand, adjusts the pH, then adds chlorine to kill germs.
Rand Water makes about 5,000 million litres a day. About 77% goes to Joburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni. It pumps into municipal reservoirs, not into homes.
Ekurhuleni buys that water and runs the reservoirs, street pipes, meters and billing. Pipes and geysers inside your property are usually the landlord's or body corporate's job.

sections.title: Why the taps run dry
points: Most Gauteng outages are not about empty dams. Experts call it an 'institutional drought': the water exists, but pumps, pipes and power fail.
Power cuts stop the pumps. On 2 November 2026 an Ekurhuleni power failure stopped Rand Water's Mapleton pump station, and Rand Water warned of shortages in Ekurhuleni.
Planned maintenance causes big cuts. Rand Water's December 2025 maintenance hit Edenvale, and the city warned that pressure can take up to two weeks to recover, especially in high-lying areas.
Demand is too high. Rand Water is licensed to take 1,600 million cubic metres a year but took 193 million more than that in 2023/24.
Leaks waste a lot. Gauteng loses about 431 billion litres a year. Ekurhuleni does better than most metros here: its losses are within international averages.

Help is coming slowly. Phase II of the Lesotho project (Polihali Dam) will raise transfers from 780 million to about 1.27 billion cubic metres a year. Water is expected around 2028 to 2030, and the date has slipped before.

sections.title: Is it safe to drink?
points: SANS 241 is South Africa's drinking water standard. It sets limits for germs, chemicals and things like cloudiness. Germs such as E. coli must be at zero.

Blue Drop is the government's audit of drinking water systems. A score above 95% earns a certificate. In the 2023 full audit, Ekurhuleni scored 97% and Joburg 98%. Only 26 systems in the whole country were certified.
The 2025 Blue Drop progress check (released March 2026) found big metros 'generally performing well', with Gauteng and the Western Cape strongest. It was a progress check, not a full audit.
Ekurhuleni's own 2024/25 report shows 98% to 100% compliance with SANS 241 across all measures.

Green Drop audits sewage treatment. In 2026 Ekurhuleni won six Green Drop certificates and took the top three wastewater spots in the country. That matters because treated sewage flows back into rivers.

You can check results yourself on the government's IRIS 'My Water' map. By law, a city must warn residents if its water is a health risk. Boil only if a notice tells you to, or if you're using stored or untreated water.

sections.title: Filtering it yourself
points: Start with the goal. Your tap water already meets the standard, so a filter here mostly fixes taste and chlorine smell. The US CDC (its national public health agency) says you may not need one at all if your water is clean.

Carbon jug filters (activated carbon traps chemicals on its surface) improve taste and chlorine and can cut some lead. They are not built to remove germs. A Brita Aluna 2.4 L jug is R699 at Yuppiechef, and a 2-pack of Maxtra Pro cartridges is R699, so about R350 per cartridge. Check the box for how often to swap it.
Tap-mounted filters screw onto the kitchen tap with no plumbing, which suits a rental. The Brita On Tap system is R1,999 at Yuppiechef.

Reverse osmosis (RO) pushes water through a very fine membrane. It removes lead, copper and salt and can cut fluoride and nitrate. It also strips minerals, sends some water down the drain and needs under-sink plumbing. Local 5-stage units start around R1,700.

UV filters use light to kill germs but don't remove chemicals. They need power and a pre-filter. They're useful for rainwater, but overkill for treated city water. Ceramic gravity filters trap dirt and many bacteria. They don't stop viruses or dissolved chemicals unless they also have a carbon core.

Check certification. NSF/ANSI (a US standards body) labels: 42 means taste and chlorine, 53 means health contaminants like lead, 58 means RO systems, 55 means UV, and 401 means newer contaminants. The numbers are not a ranking. Look up the exact model in NSF's database.

sections.title: Backup water and independence
points: Store at least 4 litres per person per day, for at least 3 days. For the two of you, that's about 24 litres minimum. Aim for about 110 litres, which covers two weeks.

Use clean, food-grade containers with tight lids. Never reuse bleach or chemical bottles. Wash them with soap and a weak bleach rinse, label them with the date, keep them cool and dark, and refill every 6 months.
A 1,000 L JoJo vertical tank costs about R1,935 at Hinterland. It needs a level, solid base. When full it weighs about a tonne, so don't put it on a balcony without checking.

In a rental, the landlord doesn't have to supply a tank, so you'd usually pay. Once installed, a tank counts as a fixture and becomes the landlord's property unless you both sign an agreement that you can take it with you.

Under the National Water Act, you can collect and use rainwater off a roof without a licence. In a flat you probably don't control the roof or gutters, so ask the body corporate. Boil or treat rainwater before drinking it.

To make water safe, bring it to a rolling boil for 1 minute. The CDC says to boil for 3 minutes only above about 2,000 m, and Edenvale sits around 1,600 m. Unscented bleach works too, but wait 30 minutes and check the strength on the label, because CDC drop counts assume 5 to 9% bleach. Neither method removes chemicals.

do: Bookmark Ekurhuleni's Outages Alert page and save the city call centre number: 0860 543 000.
Look up your area on the DWS IRIS 'My Water' map once, so you know what normal looks like.
Buy six 5 L food-grade bottles (about 30 L), fill them, write the date on them, and set a 6-month reminder to refill.
When a Rand Water maintenance notice drops for Edenvale, fill extra bottles and a bucket for flushing the day before.
Keep a way to boil water without electricity, such as a gas camping stove, because water and power cuts often come together.
Before buying a filter, decide if you want better taste (jug or tap filter) or contaminant removal (certified RO). Then check the model in NSF's database.
ask: Landlord: Can we fit a tap-mounted or under-sink filter? Can we have that in writing, including who removes it and who fixes any damage when we leave?
Landlord or body corporate: Does the building have its own storage tank or booster pump for outages? Who owns the pipes between the meter and our flat?
Body corporate: What are the rules on placing a water tank, and what weight can a balcony or yard take?
Ekurhuleni (0860 543 000): Which reservoir supplies our street? Is our area high-lying, which means slower recovery after outages?
Filter seller: Which NSF/ANSI standard is this model certified to, for which contaminants? Can I see the listing?
Filter seller: How long does a cartridge last in litres or months, what does a replacement cost, and how much water does the RO unit send down the drain?
watch_out: TDS meter and 'electrolysis' demos where tap water turns brown are sales tricks. TDS (total dissolved solids) measures minerals, not safety.
'Tested to NSF standards' is not the same as 'NSF certified'. Ask for the listing.
Alkaline and 'structured' water health claims aren't backed by solid evidence. Don't pay extra for them.
An old cartridge is worse than none. It stops working and can grow bacteria, so change it on schedule.
A full Vaal Dam doesn't mean your taps will run. Most Gauteng outages are about pumps, power and pipes.
Boiling kills germs but does nothing for fuel or chemical contamination.
Don't store drinking water in old bleach, pesticide or chemical containers, or in glass that can break.

resources.title: The Last Drop: Solving the World's Water Crisis
resources.access: Buy (Takealot / Exclusive Books, price not checked). Kindle too.
resources.why: A readable world tour of how dry places are fixing supply, so you can judge what could work in Gauteng.
takeaways: By an environmental journalist who writes for the Guardian, BBC and FT.
Treats water scarcity as the next big climate crisis.
Solutions-focused rather than doom.

resources.title: Thirst: The Global Quest to Solve the Water Crisis
resources.why: Asks who benefits from the 'global water crisis' story: a follow-the-money lens for SA water.
takeaways: A short, critical look at how the water crisis gets framed.
Focuses on celebrities, corporate charity and NGOs.
Global, not SA-specific.

resources.title: The Water Diaries: Living with the Global Water Crisis in Bangladesh and Kenya
resources.source: Sonia Hoque & Rob Hope — Cambridge University Press
resources.why: What unreliable household water looks like day to day, and how families cope.
takeaways: Tracks daily water use for a full year.
Shows how water risk changes by place and season.
Proposes a fair split of water risks between government, utilities and households.

resources.title: Great Johannesburg: What Happened? How to Save an African Economic Giant
resources.why: The municipal decay and money problems behind Joburg's failing services, water included.
takeaways: By a journalist who also worked as a municipal civil servant.
Argues Joburg is in a 'death spiral' and sets out a rescue plan.
Water comes in as part of the wider governance failure.

resources.title: Asinamanzi: Fluid Realities – Exploring South Africa's Water Crisis and Social Dynamics
resources.access: Buy (African Books Collective, price not checked)
resources.why: How ordinary South Africans cope when water is unequal and unreliable.
takeaways: A UCT anthropologist's study of water politics in Khayelitsha.
Highlights the coping strategies residents use.
Cape Town-based, so read it for the patterns, not Gauteng detail.

resources.title: Inquiry Report into the State of Water and Sanitation Service Delivery in Gauteng
resources.why: The newest official account of why Gauteng taps run dry and who is accountable. Released this month.
takeaways: Released 2 November 2026 after hearings with eight water authorities.
Some Joburg suburbs went up to 12 weeks without tap water.
Causes: ageing pipes, unrepaired leaks, too little pumping and storage, staff shortages, poor revenue collection.
Its eight recommendations are not binding.

resources.title: Water insecurity in Johannesburg (and beyond?)
resources.source: Craig Sheridan (Wits) — South African Journal of Science
resources.why: A Wits water researcher's short take on why Joburg's supply keeps failing and what to do about it.
takeaways: The author directs the Wits Centre in Water Research and Development.
Covers intermittent supply and water reclamation.
Short commentary, a quick read.

resources.title: City of Johannesburg water sector profile
resources.why: A concise research profile of Joburg's water system, with household survey data.
takeaways: 36% of people in GCRO's 2023/24 survey had water interruptions.
Water lost to leaks and non-payment is far above the 15% global benchmark.
Not read in full yet, so check the figures in the PDF.

resources.title: The prospects for rainwater harvesting at the University of Cape Town
resources.why: How to size a tank and judge whether rainwater harvesting pays off.
takeaways: Models rainwater against uses like toilet flushing, across tank sizes.
Works out savings using municipal tariffs.
Gauteng's summer-only rain will change the sums.

resources.title: Evaluation of water quality in urban drinking water networks: a case study in Johannesburg
resources.source: Lubabalo Luyaba — MSc thesis, University of Cape Town
resources.why: How old pipes and power cuts can spoil water between the treatment plant and your tap.
takeaways: Pipe age, condition and material mattered most, especially old steel, iron and clay pipes.
Higher load-shedding stages worsened water quality.
It's a computer model, not samples from homes.

resources.title: WaterCAN Gauteng water sources testing (59 sites)
resources.why: Citizen testing shows how polluted Gauteng's rivers and dams are, which is why treatment and filtering matter.
takeaways: 39 of 59 sources were unsafe to drink untreated.
All 5 dams tested had unsafe E. coli.
These are raw sources, not tap water.

resources.title: Outages Alert (City of Ekurhuleni press releases)
resources.why: Where planned and unplanned water cuts for Edenvale are posted.
takeaways: This is an archive of Ekurhuleni outage notices, rather than a complete real-time map of every supply interruption.
Its notices distinguish planned Rand Water work from local service interruptions.
The archive includes the 7 to 15 December 2025 maintenance window.
A January 2024 notice warned that restoration depended on how quickly Rand Water's system stabilised.
Check the publication date and affected places because old notices remain in the archive.

resources.title: IRIS My Water: South Africa's Tap Water Map
resources.why: Live SANS 241 compliance map. Check your area's water quality.
takeaways: DWS identifies My Water as its public route to municipal drinking-water quality information.
It uses water-quality results submitted by municipalities, so reporting completeness matters.
Use the relevant municipality and supply system rather than a national average.
The map could not be directly loaded during this research, so no present Edenvale reading is asserted here.
DWS's release confirms the monthly-data service, while 2026 reporting still identifies some IRIS datasets as assessed against SANS 241:2015.

resources.title: Rand Water
resources.why: Bulk supplier. Shows weekly water use for each metro, including Ekurhuleni.
takeaways: Rand Water provides bulk treated water to municipalities, including Ekurhuleni, before local distribution to households.
Its technical material identifies Vereeniging and Zuikerbosch as the main treatment sites.
Booster stations including Palmiet and Mapleton move treated water through the regional system.
Rand Water publishes technical and standards material that can be checked separately from municipal notices.
The homepage could not be fetched directly, so these points are corroborated by Rand Water documents and the linked outage reporting rather than a current homepage reading.

resources.title: Rand Water planned maintenance for December 2025
resources.why: A real example of a maintenance cut that hit Edenvale, and the two-week recovery warning.
takeaways: The notice concerns a historical planned-maintenance period from 7 to 15 December 2025.
Affected places included Edenvale, Bedfordview, Germiston, Thembisa, Kempton Park and several other Ekurhuleni areas on different days.
The city said it would deploy tankers and share their locations through councillors and digital channels.
It warned that pressure and supply could take up to two weeks after the work to normalise, especially in higher areas.
The original page timed out; these details were recovered from the municipal archive and Municipality News's reproduction of the notice.

resources.title: Official reports reveal massive scale of the waste, pollution and poorly treated water crisis
resources.why: 2023 Blue Drop results: Ekurhuleni 97%, Joburg 98%.
takeaways: The article reports the December 2023 release of Blue Drop, No Drop and wastewater progress findings.
It says 46% of drinking-water systems had poor or bad microbiological compliance at times during the audited 2022 period.
It reports national non-revenue water at 47%, including leaks and failures in metering and billing.
It reports 64% of wastewater works at high or critical risk of inadequately treated discharge.
Blue Drop certificates went to 26 providers, with certification requiring a score above 95%.
The national deterioration did not mean every major-city tap was unsafe; the article explicitly notes generally better metropolitan drinking-water quality.

resources.title: SA's water crisis deepens: nearly half of wastewater systems critical
resources.why: Latest Blue, Green and No Drop findings, including Gauteng's 431 billion litres of losses.
takeaways: The March 2026 article covers the 2025 full Green Drop report and Blue and No Drop progress reports.
Green Drop assessed 848 municipal wastewater systems across 144 authorities for the 2023/24 financial year.
Systems in critical condition increased from 334 in 2022 to 396 in 2025, or 47% of those assessed.
National non-revenue water remained about 47.3%.
It reports Ekurhuleni and Cape Town performing within international averages for non-revenue water.
The article cautions that audit periods prevent the reports from describing the current water quality at a particular tap.

resources.title: Water woes: what the temporary shutdown of the supply from Lesotho means for Johannesburg
resources.why: The clearest walk-through of Lesotho to Vaal to Rand Water.
takeaways: The six-month Lesotho Highlands maintenance shutdown began at midnight on 30 September 2024.
The article distinguishes a rainfall-driven drought from an institutional drought [failure to manage and deliver available water].
It reports expert disagreement with claims that the planned shutdown would itself worsen Johannesburg's municipal supply problems.
Sterkfontein serves as reserve storage for the Vaal system and loses less to evaporation than a shallower, warmer storage site.
The reasoning depends on the wider system's reserves and planning, not on treating the Vaal Dam's percentage alone as a crisis forecast.
This is a 2024 explanation of a particular shutdown, not an assessment of November 2026 supply.

resources.title: Ekurhuleni water outages as power failure leaves Rand Water unable to pump
resources.why: A recent local case of a power cut causing a water cut.
takeaways: A power interruption stopped Rand Water's Mapleton Pumping Station at about 20:35 on 2 November 2026.
The 3 November report says a breaker fault remained unresolved when Rand Water issued its statement.
Rand Water said it could not control restoration of the city's electricity supply.
It warned of shortages in Ekurhuleni, Tshwane, Lesedi, Govan Mbeki, Victor Khanye and Thembisile Hani.
The article illustrates electricity-water dependence but gives no confirmed restoration time or address-level Edenvale impact.

resources.title: About Choosing Home Water Filters
resources.why: Plain guide to what jug, under-sink and RO filters actually remove.
takeaways: CDC says a filter may improve taste, safety or both, and some households may not need one.
The right choice depends on the harmful substances actually present in the water.
Most pitcher and refrigerator filters are not designed to remove germs.
Filters can also remove useful disinfectant residuals or other substances with benefits.
Filter performance depends on pore size, substance size and interactions with the filter material.
People with weakened immune systems may need specific protection against Cryptosporidium [a parasite] and should discuss suitable treatment with their clinician.

resources.title: NSF Standards for Water Treatment Systems
resources.why: What 42, 53, 55, 58 and 401 mean. Use it with NSF's certified product search.
takeaways: NSF standard numbers identify different purposes, not a ranking from weak to strong.
NSF/ANSI 42 covers aesthetic reductions such as chlorine taste and odour.
NSF/ANSI 53 covers specific contaminants with health effects, while 58 covers RO systems.
NSF/ANSI 55 distinguishes Class A UV treatment of contaminated water from Class B supplemental treatment.
NSF/ANSI 44 concerns softeners that exchange calcium and magnesium for sodium or potassium.
Certification must be read for the particular contaminant claim and product rather than treated as permission to call any water safe.

resources.title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency
resources.why: Boiling and bleach steps, with amounts.
takeaways: CDC recommends bottled, boiled or appropriately treated water when the supply may be unsafe after an emergency.
Bring clear water to a rolling boil for one minute, or three minutes above 6,500 feet, approximately 1,981 metres.
Cloudy water should first be settled or filtered through a clean cloth or suitable paper filter before boiling.
Boiling or disinfection cannot make water with fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive contamination safe.
Cool boiled water and store it in clean, sanitised, tightly covered containers.
Local emergency instructions take priority over assuming that an ordinary household filter can handle the problem.

resources.title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply
resources.why: How much to store, which containers to use and how often to refresh them.
takeaways: The old CDC URL redirects to its updated emergency-water-storage page.
Store at least one US gallon, about 3.8 litres, per person daily for three days.
CDC suggests building towards two weeks of supply where possible.
Store more for hot conditions, illness, pregnancy and pets as needed.
Replace water filled into home containers every six months and observe dates on commercially bottled water.
Use food-grade containers that can be cleaned and tightly closed, and avoid containers that previously held toxic substances.

resources.title: The quest for generators, inverters and water tanks
resources.why: Who pays for a tank in a rental, and who owns it afterwards.
takeaways: This 2022 property article focuses on who pays for backup equipment in rental properties.
It explains that electricity interruptions can prevent reservoir filling and disrupt sewage works.
The article says landlords are not automatically obliged to supply generators, inverters or tanks for utility failures outside their control.
It presents backup equipment as a possible property improvement that may attract tenants or higher rent.
It says a tenant may need to fund requested equipment when the landlord will not provide it.
Those are the article's broad legal assertions, not a current ruling on a specific lease; the page is not a technical tank-sizing guide.

resources.title: National Water Act, Schedule 1: Permissible use of water
resources.why: The law that lets you store and use roof rainwater without a licence.
takeaways: Schedule 1 permits reasonable domestic water use where the person has lawful access to the resource.
It permits small non-commercial gardening and specified animal watering, subject to limits protecting the resource and other users.
It expressly permits storing and using runoff from a roof.
It allows emergency abstraction for human consumption or firefighting.
Its permissions remain subject to the National Water Act and do not remove municipal plumbing, borehole or drinking-water rules.
It is not a blanket right to unlimited groundwater abstraction, commercial supply or selling water.

resources.title: Brita range (jugs, cartridges, On Tap)
resources.why: Local prices: Aluna jug R699, 2-pack of cartridges R699, On Tap R1,999.
takeaways: The retailer lists distinct jug, tap-mounted and replacement-cartridge product ranges.
The accessed listing priced a 3.5-litre Marella jug at R799 and a 2.4-litre Aluna jug at R699.
A pack of two MAXTRA Pro cartridges was listed at R699.
The On Tap V-MF system was R1,999 and its replacement cartridge R899.
Prices are a dated retail snapshot and can change; replacement-cartridge cost belongs in the comparison.
The category page itself does not establish model-specific microbiological purification or contaminant certification.

resources.title: Vertical Water Tank 1000L JoJo
resources.why: About R1,935 for a 1,000 L tank, plus base requirements.
takeaways: The product is a stationary 1,000-litre vertical JoJo storage tank.
The accessed price was R1,934.83 including VAT, which is the tank listing rather than a complete installed backup system.
The page requires a sound, level, smooth base and says the tank must remain stationary when full.
Its concrete-base guidance specifies an ideal minimum thickness of 85 mm and a bed 100 mm wider than the tank diameter.
Listed features include a 10-year warranty, a UV-stabilised outer layer, a food-grade inner layer and a black layer intended to limit algae.
These material and storage claims do not mean the tank disinfects whatever water enters it.

resources.title: The Big Thirst: The Secret Life and Turbulent Future of Water
resources.why: A readable, fun look at how water really works and why it's getting scarce.
takeaways: The publisher describes Fishman's book as an examination of the end of assumptions that water is endlessly abundant, cheap and safe.
Its cases include Las Vegas hotels, Australian rice farming and highly purified water used in IBM manufacturing.
The reading guide highlights water's hidden roles in industry, food production and everyday technology.
It invites comparison of desalination and wastewater reuse, including their costs and public acceptance.
It links better management to understanding water's physical behaviour and social value.
This breakdown uses the publisher's description and reading guide, rather than claiming a full-text review of the book.

resources.title: Water: A Biography
resources.why: How control of water shaped societies, from ancient irrigation to modern dams.
takeaways: Boccaletti combines environmental and social history across several millennia.
The publisher's synopsis begins with settled farmers around the Nile, Tigris and Euphrates.
It connects adaptation to changing water conditions with the development of social organisation.
The book moves from ancient societies towards modern public institutions and infrastructure.
The first edition appeared in 2021, and the listed paperback followed in 2022 at 400 pages.
These are synopsis-level themes, not evidence about present Ekurhuleni water quality or a substitute for the full text.

resources.title: South Africa's Water Predicament: Freshwater's Unceasing Decline
resources.why: The SA-specific deep dive on why water services keep declining. Academic, but direct.
takeaways: Anja du Plessis evaluates deterioration in South African freshwater resources and services over roughly three decades.
The publisher's overview identifies weak governance, reactive management and dysfunctional local government as central themes.
The chapter list treats fragmented governance and questionable decisions separately from physical resource problems.
The book uses South African cases to connect water quality, infrastructure and service delivery.
Its stated goal is to prioritise urgent problems and identify actions involving political leadership, researchers and civil society.
The accessible material was the overview and contents of the 2023 book; subscription chapters were not independently reviewed.

resources.title: Day Zero: One City's Response to a Record-Breaking Drought
resources.why: How Cape Town avoided running dry, and lessons for Gauteng households.
takeaways: Leonie Joubert and Gina Ziervogel document Cape Town's response to a three-year drought.
The website explains how a climate shock collided with ordinary development and city-management pressures.
Its five perspectives include a water manager, politicians, a spokesperson, knowledge brokers and a researcher.
It treats citizen and business responses as part of the story alongside municipal administration.
A free book download and individual online chapters make it accessible without purchasing a copy.
Cape Town offers lessons about communication and adaptation, but its drought and supply geography differ from Gauteng's distribution failures.

resources.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project Turns 40: Beyond Dams, Water and Infrastructure
resources.why: 7-minute look at the scheme your tap water starts in.
takeaways: Verification gap: the supplied YouTube page could not be fetched and searches did not independently recover this exact video.
The stated title alone does not verify the speaker, producer, running time or claims.
No numerical or historical claims are attributed to the unseen video in this breakdown.
Use the verified LHDA project page, original treaty and Lesotho compensation reporting in the new resources for this topic until the video can be checked.

resources.title: Zuikerbosch Water Purification Plant to boost water supply: Majodina
resources.why: 2-minute news clip on the Rand Water plant that treats Gauteng's water.
takeaways: SABC News published this report on 26 March 2025 about Minister Pemmy Majodina's visit to Zuikerbosch.
Its description says the project then under construction cost R3.9 billion.
It presents the upgrade as supporting Rand Water supply across four provinces.
The description claims 1.2 million additional litres daily, a suspicious unit figure that conflicts with Rand Water documents describing the broader 1,200-megalitre programme.
Do not silently convert that description into a verified current capacity or commissioning result.
Only the indexed video description was available, so this is not a transcript-based assessment of what the interview actually said.

resources.title: How Water Towers Work
resources.why: Clear explainer on storage and pressure, and why high-lying areas dry up first. The whole channel is worth following.
takeaways: Practical Engineering published the 10 minute 59 second video on 10 December 2018.
The verified description concerns the purpose and function of elevated water storage tanks.
The associated learning material highlights water pressure as one of the main ideas.
It also identifies water towers' role in meeting changing demand across the day.
Use it to understand storage and pressure, while checking local network documents for which structure actually serves an Edenvale address.
The description and independent learning outline were verified, but the complete video transcript was not available during this research.

resources.title: Reverse Osmosis vs Carbon Filters: Which One Do You Actually Need?
resources.why: Short comparison of RO and carbon. Made by a filter brand, so watch for the sales angle.
takeaways: Verification gap: the exact supplied YouTube video could not be fetched or independently identified by its ID.
Searches found several similarly titled commercial articles, which do not verify this video's author or contents.
No removal percentages, operating costs or product recommendations are attributed to the unseen video.
Use the verified CDC treatment explanation and NSF certification sources in this track for the carbon-versus-RO comparison until the exact video is available.

resources.title: Water and Sanitation releases 2023 full Blue Drop Report
resources.source: Department of Water and Sanitation / South African Government
resources.why: Read the regulator's own explanation before using national crisis headlines to judge an Edenvale tap.
takeaways: The release separates drinking-water quality, wastewater management and water losses into three assessments.
National non-revenue water rose from 37% in 2014 to 47% in 2023.
It reports approximately 218 litres per person daily nationally, compared with an international reference of 173 litres.
The wastewater progress assessment placed 64% of works at high or critical risk of discharging inadequately treated water.
DWS required corrective action plans from authorities with critically performing systems.

resources.title: Why do Joburg's taps keep running dry?
resources.why: Connects individual outages to maintenance records, budgets and institutional responsibility.
takeaways: The Gauteng dashboard recorded 50,536 Johannesburg pipe leaks between June 2025 and June 2026.
Johannesburg reported losing more than 207 billion litres in the 2025 financial year.
The Auditor-General criticised inadequate maintenance planning, execution and oversight.
The article examines municipal sweeping accounts [transfers into the city's central bank account] and questions about returning cash to water operations.
These are Johannesburg findings, so they explain regional mechanisms without establishing Ekurhuleni's own loss rate.

resources.title: Joburg won't name its water tanker suppliers despite spending R650m in five years
resources.source: Seth Thorne / GroundUp, republished by Daily Maverick
resources.why: Shows how to investigate emergency-water spending through named contracts and disclosure requests.
takeaways: Johannesburg disclosed more than R650 million in tanker spending over five years.
Johannesburg Water told the reporter to use a formal access-to-information application for additional procurement details.
The article identifies R132 million in 2024/25 tanker spending, compared with a R1.2 billion capital budget.
Its annual-report evidence includes R817,000 in irregular spending on services supplied without an official purchase order.
Officials described plans to reduce reliance on outside tanker contractors, but those plans were commitments rather than completed results.

resources.title: SAHRC warns Gauteng water crisis is about failing infrastructure, not a lack of water
resources.why: Provides unusually useful Ekurhuleni findings and distinguishes allegations from the inquiry's conclusions.
takeaways: The inquiry covered Gauteng's nine water services authorities.
It reported Ekurhuleni water losses of about 25.4%, valued at R1.27 billion.
About one quarter of Ekurhuleni reservoirs had less than 24 hours of storage capacity.
It reported a wastewater Green Drop score of 81.7% and seven of 17 assessed treatment works at or above design capacity.
The report found insufficient evidence to conclude that tanker procurement was corrupt, despite strong public criticism of tankering.
It also said the evidence did not independently establish unlawful or improper diversion of Johannesburg Water revenue.

resources.title: Joburg awards R263m water tanker tender to two 20-somethings
resources.why: An investigative case study of how bidder relationships and equipment ownership deserve scrutiny.
takeaways: The investigation concerns an estimated R263 million, three-year tanker contract.
Builtpro and Nutinox were the two selected companies.
The reporting questions addresses used by bidders and apparent connections between competing businesses.
It investigates plans to lease equipment from Astron Fleet, linked to established operator Aqua Transport and Plant Hire.
It also identifies an earlier six-month emergency contract worth R69 million involving Builtpro and Kukhulu.
This is the original 2024 investigation; the later 2026 reporting is needed for the court ruling and appeal context.

resources.title: Stakeholders press LHDA on compensation, grazing land and local opportunity as water project turns 40
resources.source: Thoboloko Ntšonyane and Seabata Mahao / Newsday Lesotho
resources.why: Adds the voices and costs on the Lesotho side of Gauteng's water infrastructure.
takeaways: Affected residents raised compensation, environmental protection and procurement concerns at the October stakeholder conference.
Phase II is designed to increase annual transfers from 780 million cubic metres to more than 1.27 billion.
The article reports R24 billion spent from a R53 billion allocation at that stage.
It cites an Ombudsman finding of more than M142 million in Phase I compensation arrears by the end of 2025.
Reported Phase II arrears were about M6.7 million; M denotes Lesotho maloti, linked at parity to the Rand.
Construction progress and unresolved community claims can coexist, so one should not be used to dismiss the other.

resources.title: New Ekurhuleni tariffs effective from 1 July 2026
resources.why: Establishes the approved increase rather than the earlier draft proposal.
takeaways: The approved water-tariff increase is 11% from 1 July 2026.
The sanitation increase is 8.35%, so it should be checked separately on a household bill.
The city places the adjustments within an annual budget of R70.9 billion.
The notice says final increases followed public consultation and affordability concerns.
It directs qualifying residents towards indigent support and debt-rehabilitation incentives.
The percentage announcement does not replace the detailed tariff schedule needed to calculate a particular bill.

resources.title: Application process of installing a borehole
resources.why: The practical municipal process that a generic national borehole guide can miss.
takeaways: The city says permission is mandatory before drilling starts.
Owners request the application form and submit supporting documents to the listed municipal contacts.
Applications go to City Planning's Dolomite Section for geological and hydrological review.
The Water Demand Management Section considers the review before an approval or rejection letter is prepared.
The Head of Department signs the final letter, so a submitted application is not itself permission to drill.
The notice contains a mistaken Act-number reference; the National Water Act is Act 36 of 1998.

resources.title: About Home Water Treatment Systems
resources.source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
resources.why: A non-sales explanation of which treatment mechanisms handle which problems.
takeaways: Point-of-use treatment serves one outlet, while point-of-entry treatment serves most or all of the home.
RO uses a membrane and pressure to reduce germs and selected dissolved chemicals.
UV treatment works better with prefiltration and can inactivate parasites, bacteria and viruses.
UV does not remove chemicals, so it cannot solve every borehole-quality problem.
Water softeners primarily remove calcium and magnesium and do not disinfect water.
The page recommends testing and matching treatment to the actual hazard rather than installing equipment automatically.

resources.title: Collecting Rainwater and Your Health: An Overview
resources.source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
resources.why: Explains why apparently clean roof water needs a separate safety assessment.
takeaways: Airborne dust and smoke can contaminate rain before it reaches a roof.
Roofing, gutters, pipes and storage materials can add chemicals to collected water.
Bird droppings and accumulated roof dirt can enter tanks, especially after dry weather.
Mixing untreated rainwater with treated water can contaminate the treated supply.
CDC recommends regular microbial and chemical testing when rainwater is used for drinking, cooking or bathing.
Its US legal references do not establish what is allowed in Ekurhuleni; use the municipal bylaw for that.

resources.title: Lesotho Highlands Development Authority: project, dam and royalty updates
resources.why: Bookmark the implementing authority for dated progress, procurement and Lesotho-side information.
takeaways: The project was established by a treaty signed in 1986.
Its purposes include supplying Gauteng with water and generating hydropower for Lesotho.
Phase I was completed in 2003 and inaugurated in 2004.
The homepage's 1 October 2026 update lists Polihali Dam at 56% and the transfer tunnel at 60%.
It publishes separately dated Katse and Mohale storage readings, plus royalty and procurement links.
These construction percentages describe progress at a date, rather than proving that Phase II water is already reaching households.

resources.title: National Hydrological Services: dams, floods and flows
resources.why: The primary source for checking regional water availability independently of outage notices.
takeaways: The portal separates audited historical data from unaudited near-real-time measurements and forecasts.
Its weekly State of Dams service covers approximately 210 dams.
Vaal and Orange services provide daily flows, levels and rainfall information.
Flood tools show actual and predicted levels and routed flows through major dams.
A dam percentage is a storage measurement, not a water-quality result or a measure of pressure in a municipal reservoir.

resources.title: NSF official listings: drinking-water treatment units, health effects
resources.why: Verify an exact model's certified claims before spending money on a health-related filter claim.
takeaways: This listing concerns NSF/ANSI 53, which covers specified health-related contaminant reductions.
Entries identify manufacturers, model names and, where relevant, replacement elements.
Tables show service capacity and flow rate alongside individual reduction claims.
Claims differ between products, including lead, cysts, particular pesticides and other substances.
Some arsenic claims carry restrictions about concentration and chemical form.
NSF warns about altered copies of its listings, so verify status on the official site rather than a seller's screenshot.

resources.title: Groundwater: Frequently Asked Questions
resources.why: Clarifies the national distinction between registering a water use and registering a physical borehole.
takeaways: DWS explains that national registration concerns the water use, not simply the existence of a borehole.
Schedule 1 household use does not require national water-use registration, but municipal borehole rules can still apply.
Uses beyond Schedule 1 need consideration under the relevant national authorisation route.
The FAQ recommends chemical testing before using groundwater as a domestic supply.
It distinguishes a borehole's pumping yield from a sustainable abstraction rate [how much can be taken over time].
The page uses older departmental names, so it is background guidance rather than a substitute for a current municipal application.

resources.title: Water quality assessment of rooftop harvested rainwater across different roof types in a semi-arid region of South Africa
resources.source: Livhuwani and colleagues / Water Environment Research
resources.why: Local measured evidence against assuming that clear rainwater or a good chemistry score means safe drinking water.
takeaways: The study compared aluminium, slate, steel and concrete roofs around the University of Venda, Sibasa and Tshikhudini.
Reported average E. coli levels in Tshikhudini ranged from 4.31 to 11.56 colony-forming units per 100 ml across roof types.
The authors found microbial results above drinking-water limits even though measured chemical quality was generally acceptable.
October 2021 first-flush samples carried the highest E. coli contamination after accumulated dirt was washed off roofs.
Including E. coli in the water-quality index changed the assessment, exposing the weakness of an index that omits microbial risk.
These Limpopo findings explain plausible hazards but do not measure the quality of a particular Edenvale roof or tank.

resources.title: 1986 treaty on the Lesotho Highlands Water Project
resources.source: Governments of Lesotho and South Africa / FAO treaty collection
resources.why: The primary agreement behind the transfer system and its royalty economics.
takeaways: The treaty was signed at Maseru on 24 October 1986.
It establishes obligations for developing the shared Highlands project and delivering water to South Africa.
Article 12 allocates the calculated net benefit for Sub-phase IA as 56% to Lesotho and 44% to South Africa.
The calculation compares the project with an alternative Orange-Vaal transfer scheme.
Royalties include fixed and variable components linked to investment, electricity and other operating savings.
This original treaty is historical primary evidence; later agreements and current royalty reports are needed for present project terms and amounts.

resources.title: Water for All: Global Solutions for a Changing Climate
resources.why: A practical global complement to the South African governance material, written by a water-treatment researcher.
takeaways: The publisher's description identifies outdated infrastructure and ineffective policy alongside climate change and population growth.
The book examines efficiency improvements as one route to resolving shortages.
It includes communities that used crises to address longstanding water-rights disputes.
Its treatment options include desalination, wastewater recycling and capturing more rainfall in cities and fields.
The author directs the Berkeley Water Center and teaches civil and environmental engineering.
This breakdown is based on the publisher's synopsis, not a claim to have verified every argument in the 440-page book.

resources.title: How Sewage Recycling Works
resources.why: The creator's page includes the video and transcript, making its engineering claims easier to inspect.
takeaways: Wichita Falls developed emergency drinking-water reuse after severe drought reduced its reservoirs.
Indirect reuse routes treated water through a river, lake or aquifer before abstraction and purification.
Direct reuse removes that environmental buffer, so engineered monitoring, alarms, shutdowns and redundant barriers become especially important.
Its emergency process used wastewater treatment, RO and conventional drinking-water treatment in sequence.
The project operated for a year from July 2014 and reclaimed nearly 2 billion US gallons.
The case shows what controlled reuse requires; it does not imply that untreated sewage in a river is safe.

resources.title: Guidelines for drinking-water quality: fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda
resources.why: The evidence framework behind national drinking-water rules, with chapters for specific hazards.
takeaways: WHO recommends health-based targets, catchment-to-consumer water safety plans and independent surveillance.
Separate chapters cover microbial, chemical, radiological and acceptability questions.
The 2022 update added or revised guidance for cyanobacterial toxins [toxins produced by some aquatic bacteria].
The update also revised guidance for manganese and several industrial chemicals.
The guidelines inform national standards but do not replace South African legal requirements.
The 614-page reference is best used to inspect a named hazard rather than read as a general lifestyle book.

resources.title: WaterWazi: explore South African water data
resources.why: A visual way to locate treatment works, receiving rivers and the underlying monitoring evidence.
takeaways: The map supports navigation through provinces, districts, municipalities and wards.
Treatment works can be filtered by microbial, chemical, physical and operational compliance.
Filters include monitoring year, responsible institution and the receiving water body.
Individual works show capacity, class, compliance percentages and source information.
The interface links to DWS river, effluent and potable-water data.
Check each record's year and source before treating a mapped status as a current condition.

resources.title: Ekurhuleni amended Water Services By-laws
resources.why: Read the actual local provisions for drinking rainwater, boreholes, tanks and sewer charges.
takeaways: Section 70(2) prohibits using water collected in rainwater tanks as potable water.
Section 71 requires written approval before drilling a new borehole or deepening an existing one.
Section 71(9) prohibits sinking a borehole in a dolomite area.
Borehole drinking water must meet relevant standards, and blending it with municipal water is prohibited.
Section 71(15) allows sewer charges or borehole metering when alternative water enters the municipal sanitation network.
Section 39(3) requires regular cleaning and maintenance of potable storage tanks at intervals no longer than two years; more frequent attention may be needed in practice.

resources.title: ERWAT Business Plan 2022/23 to 2026/27
resources.why: Maps the less visible wastewater half of Ekurhuleni's water system and its operating constraints.
takeaways: The plan describes ERWAT operating 19 water care works in four drainage districts.
The works receive both domestic and industrial wastewater.
Individual design capacities range from 1 to 170 megalitres daily [1 megalitre is 1 million litres].
DWS water-use licences govern effluent quality, discharge quantities, sludge management and reporting.
The plan identifies capacity limits, equipment failures and power failures among operational challenges.
Its proposed regionalisation [combining treatment into fewer larger facilities] and expansion are plans, not proof of achieved performance.

resources.title: Migrating from SANS 241:2015 to SANS 241:2025: Practical implications
resources.why: A technical operator's explanation of why a passing sample is only one part of water safety.
takeaways: The presentation contrasts the older two-part standard with the integrated 2025 edition.
It links numerical limits, risk assessment, monitoring, corrective action and evidence of control.
Monitoring distinguishes mandatory process parameters from additional parameters selected through system-specific risk assessment.
The contents explicitly address borehole systems, mobile tankers and static tanks.
It stresses that missing monitoring data undermines the ability to demonstrate control.
This is explanatory training material, not the normative standard; apparent unit errors on individual slides should not be copied into household specifications.

resources.title: Technical report for additional raw-water abstraction: Rand Water purification systems
resources.source: Rand Water water-use licence application / Department of Water and Sanitation repository
resources.why: Section 20 documents the actual local treatment chain rather than generic filter advertising.
takeaways: Section 20 identifies Vereeniging and Zuikerbosch as the two main treatment plants drawing from the Vaal system.
It describes flocculation and sedimentation [clumping particles and letting them settle] before filtration.
Carbon dioxide adjusts pH before rapid gravity sand filtration.
Chlorination precedes pumping to Eikenhof, Zwartkopjes, Palmiet or Mapleton booster stations.
At boosters, ammonia and chlorine form a longer-lasting disinfectant for distribution.
A treatment-process description explains intended barriers; separate monitoring data are needed to establish achieved quality.

who_pays: Ekurhuleni households and businesses pay municipal water charges, while the city buys treated bulk water from Rand Water.
The bill supports several layers: raw-water infrastructure, treatment, electricity for pumping, local pipes and reservoirs, and administration.
Sanitation is a separate service charge, and ERWAT treats much of Ekurhuleni's wastewater on the city's behalf.
National grants and municipal support policies help fund infrastructure and services for qualifying poor households, so access to a basic allocation does not make treatment costless.
Outages create a second household bill through bottled water, tanks, pumps, filters, maintenance and time spent collecting water.
who_decides: The Department of Water and Sanitation [DWS] manages national water resources, regulates water use and oversees drinking-water and wastewater performance.
South Africa and Lesotho govern their shared Highlands project through a treaty, while LHDA implements the Lesotho-side works and TCTA has South African project responsibilities.
Rand Water treats and transports bulk water, while Ekurhuleni is the water services authority [the municipality responsible for ensuring local access].
The municipal council approves retail tariffs and budgets after public consultation, and city departments operate local distribution and approve borehole applications.

SANS 241 [South Africa's drinking-water standard] defines quality and management requirements, but a published standard needs sampling, competent operators and enforcement to protect a particular tap.
who_profits: Rand Water is a public utility, so its revenue and surplus must be distinguished from a private company's shareholder profit.
Lesotho receives treaty royalties, and its electricity system benefits from hydropower associated with the project.
Construction companies, engineering firms, electricity suppliers, lenders and chemical suppliers earn revenue from building and operating water infrastructure.
Bottled-water sellers, tanker contractors, borehole drillers and filtration installers gain business when residents lose confidence in public supply.

Investigations document questionable tanker procurement, but financial incentives alone do not prove sabotage; the 2026 SAHRC inquiry said its evidence was insufficient to conclude that tanker procurement was corrupt.
what_it_means_for_us: In Edenvale, separate three questions: is water available in the Vaal system, can the network deliver it, and is the water reaching our tap safe?
Use notices for the actual suburb and reservoir zone, then read recent local laboratory results alongside the sample date and location.
Store a small protected drinking-water reserve separately from water intended for toilets and cleaning, and size any larger tank around measured household use.
Choose filtration for a demonstrated problem and a verified model-specific claim; a chlorine-taste filter is not an emergency disinfection system.
Check Ekurhuleni's rules before drilling or connecting alternative supplies, and budget for recurring costs rather than treating a tank or borehole as permanent independence.

deep_sections.title: Why full dams can still mean dry taps
points: The Integrated Vaal River System [linked dams, rivers and transfer schemes] supplies a region much larger than Ekurhuleni.
Lesotho Highlands transfers enter South Africa through the Ash River and feed the wider Vaal system; they do not run through a dedicated pipe to an Edenvale kitchen.
Katse and Mohale store water in Lesotho, while Sterkfontein provides reserve storage for the Vaal system.
The 2024 Lesotho tunnel shutdown was planned maintenance, so its existence alone did not establish a shortage at Johannesburg taps.
Rand Water's main treatment sites are Vereeniging and Zuikerbosch, followed by booster stations that push water towards higher ground.
Coagulation [making fine particles clump], settling and sand filtration remove suspended material before disinfection.
Rand Water also uses chloramination [adding ammonia to chlorine to form a longer-lasting disinfectant] in its distribution process.
Electricity failure can stop pumping even when raw water and treatment capacity are available.
A municipal reservoir is a short-term buffer, so its usable storage can run down during a prolonged interruption.
Recovery requires incoming flow to exceed current demand, which explains why restoring a pump does not instantly refill every reservoir.
Higher areas may recover later because delivering water uphill requires enough pressure [force pushing water through pipes].
The November 2026 Mapleton outage illustrates dependence on municipal electricity, but the report does not establish that every Edenvale property uses that station.
For a local outage, ask which reservoir supplies the address, what failed, whether pumping has resumed and whether reservoir levels are recovering.

deep_sections.title: What water scores actually prove
points: Blue Drop evaluates drinking-water systems, Green Drop evaluates wastewater systems, and No Drop evaluates water-use efficiency and losses.
A Green Drop failure means sewage management needs attention; it does not itself show that treated household drinking water failed a test.
An audit score combines management and operational evidence, so it is different from the percentage of samples meeting a contaminant limit.
The 2023 finding that 46% of systems had poor or bad microbiological compliance describes systems and an earlier sampling period, not 46% of all glasses of water today.
Read the assessment year, sampling period and release date separately; the 2025 Green Drop report released in 2026 assessed the 2023/24 municipal year.
SANS 241:2025 strengthens risk management, monitoring and incident response, while historical datasets can still identify SANS 241:2015 as their reporting basis.
E. coli [a bacterium used as an indicator of faecal contamination] is a warning signal, not a test for every possible pathogen.
A TDS meter [a meter estimating total dissolved solids from conductivity] cannot establish whether water contains harmful bacteria or every toxic chemical.
Taste, smell and clarity matter for acceptability, but clear water can still contain germs and an unfamiliar taste does not identify the cause.
Request the sample location, date, result, units, applicable limit and laboratory method rather than accepting an undated claim of SANS compliance.
Use a laboratory whose accreditation covers the relevant water tests, and follow its bottle, transport and holding-time instructions.
A passing sample before a storage tank does not establish the quality after that tank or after an overdue household filter.
Low or negative pressure can draw contamination through leaks or unsafe cross-connections [links between drinking and non-drinking pipes].
An international review linked outages with gastrointestinal illness, but its pooled estimates cannot calculate this household's risk or explain an individual pregnancy loss.

deep_sections.title: Buy treatment for the actual hazard
points: Activated carbon works mainly by adsorption [substances sticking to a large internal surface], and its performance depends on the material, contact time and cartridge condition.
A jug sold for chlorine taste should not be assumed to remove bacteria, nitrate, arsenic or all metals.
Some certified carbon systems reduce lead or particular PFAS [persistent industrial chemicals], so claims that carbon can never remove them are also misleading.
Chloramine reduction is a separate performance question from ordinary chlorine reduction, which matters when checking equipment for Rand Water supply.
RO [reverse osmosis] forces water through a membrane to reduce many dissolved substances, but the complete system still needs the right certification and maintenance.
RO also produces concentrate [water carrying rejected substances], so compare litres rejected per litre delivered at the actual operating pressure.
UV [ultraviolet light] inactivates germs when the delivered dose is adequate; it does not remove dissolved chemical pollution.
Cloudiness, lamp ageing, dirty sleeves and excessive flow can undermine UV performance, so prefiltration and a working failure alarm matter.
NSF/ANSI 42 concerns aesthetic claims [taste, odour and similar qualities], while 53 concerns specified health-related reductions and 58 covers RO systems.
NSF/ANSI 55 distinguishes Class A disinfection systems from Class B systems used for supplemental treatment of already disinfected water.
A standard number is not a universal contaminant guarantee; check the exact system, cartridge, reduction claim, rated flow and service life in a certifier's listing.
A point-of-use system [treatment at one drinking tap] can keep operating costs lower when the identified issue concerns drinking and cooking water.
Removing disinfectant before long storage or a whole-house pipe network creates a new maintenance responsibility because the residual protection is reduced.
Compare five-year ownership costs in Rands, including installation, cartridges, electricity, laboratory checks, sanitation and RO reject water.
During a boil-water advisory, follow the advisory even if a household jug is installed; boiling cannot make chemically contaminated water safe.

deep_sections.title: Storage, rain and groundwater are different systems
points: A municipal backup tank stores previously treated water, while a rainwater tank collects a new raw-water source with different contamination risks.
CDC's emergency baseline is about 3.8 litres per person daily for three days, covering drinking and limited essential uses rather than normal showers and laundry.
For two people, that baseline is about 23 litres for three days; this is a calculation, and heat, illness or other needs can increase it.
Estimate larger-tank endurance as usable litres divided by measured daily demand; 1,000 usable litres at 200 litres per day lasts five days by calculation.
A full 1,000-litre tank holds roughly one tonne of water before the tank's own weight, so the base and supporting structure matter.
Use protected openings, suitable potable-water materials and a cleaning plan, and prevent a booster pump from creating an unsafe connection to the municipal main.
Keep stored drinking water in clean, closed containers and avoid dipping hands or cups into the supply.
CDC advises replacing self-filled emergency container water every six months; this is separate from managing a permanently plumbed tank.
Rainwater yield depends on roof area, rainfall and collection losses; 1 mm of rain on 1 square metre represents 1 litre before losses.
A first-flush diverter [a device discarding the first dirty roof runoff] reduces contamination but does not establish drinking-water safety.
The South African rooftop study found microbial contamination despite generally acceptable chemical results, so a good chemical score was not enough.
National Schedule 1 allows storage and use of roof runoff, but municipal rules still govern safe plumbing and drinking use.
Section 70(2) of Ekurhuleni's published amended bylaw prohibits using water collected in rainwater tanks as potable water [water for drinking].
Ekurhuleni's published rules require prior approval for new boreholes and prohibit sinking them in dolomite areas [rock terrain vulnerable to ground instability].
A national Schedule 1 household water use does not remove municipal drilling requirements, and a higher-volume or commercial use may need a different national authorisation.
A borehole's pumping rate does not prove a sustainable long-term supply or safe chemistry, and groundwater used indoors can still attract sewer charges.

deep_sections.title: Follow the money without inventing a conspiracy
points: Non-revenue water [supplied water that does not generate billed revenue] includes physical leaks, meter and accounting errors, and authorised unbilled use.
Unpaid bills are a related cash-collection problem, but technically billed water does not become non-revenue water merely because a customer has not paid.
Several public summaries blur those categories, so ask for the utility's water balance [an accounting of where supplied water goes].
Fixing a real leak saves treated water and pumping costs, while improving a faulty meter can raise revenue without saving the same physical volume.
The municipality pays upstream for treated water even when a local leak prevents it from reaching a paying customer.
Ekurhuleni announced an 11% water-tariff increase and an 8.35% sanitation increase from 1 July 2026 after consultation.
The earlier draft proposed a larger water increase, so a draft budget PDF is not evidence of the final household tariff.
A block tariff [a different price for each usage band] requires adding the charge for each band rather than pricing the whole month's use at the highest band reached.
A useful bill comparison separates consumption, fixed charges, VAT, sanitation and any qualifying household subsidy.
The Lesotho treaty shares a calculated benefit from the transfer scheme through royalties; it is more complex than buying every litre at a single shop price.
People losing land or grazing access in Lesotho can bear costs even when national royalties rise, which is why compensation reporting belongs beside engineering progress.
A lucrative tanker contract is a reason to inspect procurement, delivery records and conflicts of interest, not proof that a specific pipe was deliberately broken.
Compare investigative allegations, court findings, official replies and later appeal outcomes instead of treating them as the same kind of evidence.
For accountability, track repair completion, water losses, reservoir recovery and current test results alongside money spent; a new committee or dashboard is not a repaired pipe.
